schools.summary: Henry frames the speech as a second proof of Job's weakness and inclines, against the received view, to the whale — larger and nobler, singled out in Gen. 1:21, set in the sea, the leviathan of Ps. 104:26.
Gill lays whale, crocodile, and orca side by side and reads the name (than + levi, from the close joining of the scales) to 'bid fairest for the crocodile.'
Clarke holds the description suits only the crocodile of the Nile, and proves from Herodotus that crocodiles were caught with a baited hook.
Ellicott finds 'little doubt' the crocodile is meant, keeping the AV reading of the tongue against 'press down his tongue with a cord.'

debates.question: What manner of creature is leviathan?

sides.position: the whale — larger, nobler, singled out at the creation and set in the sea
the crocodile of the Nile, whose scaled hide the name and the fishing best fit
the toothed orca, a great fish of the whale-kind

themes: canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the range of the word leviathan (celestial dragon in ch. 3:8, the whale in Ps. 104:26, the crocodile-emblem of Pharaoh in Ps. 74:13), noting the OT has no proper name for the crocodile; Ellicott glosses 'cord of rush' and 'spike or hook.'
Gill takes the 'hook' of the nose to be a rush-rope, such as Pliny says the ancients made.
Clarke sets the ring in the nose against the Eastern custom of leading oxen, and reads the thorn of stringing a fish or of harness-ornaments.
Henry folds the verse into the proof that Job had no bait, hook, line, or thorn to catch and carry the beast.

themes: leading the beast like an ox

schools.summary: Gill hears the absurdity: the creature is too spirited and stout-hearted to make supplications or sue for gentle usage; such begging is beneath it.
Clarke owns honestly that 'there are several allusions in these verses to matters of which we know nothing.'
Henry: the beast 'knows his own strength too well' to cry for quarter or covenant to be a servant to save its life.

themes: no soft words from the beast
the divine irony of the taunt
the mirror of Job's demands on God

schools.summary: Gill reads the covenant as one of friendship or servitude, by which the creature would enter Job's household and serve him.
Clarke hears in 'a servant for ever' the law of the Hebrew bondman whose ear is bored to abide in the house for ever (Exod. 21:6).
Ellicott settles it with a word: the crocodile is 'probably quite untameable,' so no covenant is possible.
Henry keeps his frame — Job could not reduce the beast to service; it would never covenant to be his perpetual servant.

themes: will he make a covenant with thee
no terms with the beast or its Maker

schools.summary: Gill catches the joke in 'play': the leviathan sports in the sea, its own element, but there is no playing with him by land, in hand or cage.
Clarke draws the domestic picture — a pet for the maidens — behind the ancient and execrable custom of tying birds by the leg for children.
Henry states the point: 'the leviathan is not one of these; he is made to be the terror, not the sport and diversion, of mankind.'

themes: wilt thou play with him as with a bird
the ascending series of failed mastery
a power no child of man commands

schools.summary: Gill reads the 'banquet' as its own denial — the beast is not to be taken; and notes crocodile flesh is eaten and savoury, whale flesh not.
Clarke: could they feast on him as on a camel, or sell his flesh? — citing Herodotus that crocodiles were eaten at Apollonople and Elephantis.
Ellicott renders 'shall the bands of fishermen make traffic of him?' as suiting the parallel with the merchants better than 'dig a pit.'
Henry reads the failure to enrich with the spoil — 'shall they part him among the merchants?' — noting whale-fishing was not yet perfected in Job's day.

themes: shall they make a banquet of him

schools.summary: Gill weighs the verse for the identity: harpoons pierce the whale, but the crocodile's scaled hide is impenetrable; the alternative 'fill ships with his skin' tells again against the whale.
Clarke reads harpoon-work, but insists the crocodile's back cannot be pierced — Herrera saw one take six musket-balls unwounded, vulnerable only under the belly.
Keil and Delitzsch gather the concluding inference: if one creature admits no attack, how much more the Creator — 'who is it who could stand before Me?' None has any claim on God.
Henry: Job could not destroy the beast or fill his head with fish-spears, for it keeps out of the reach of the instruments of slaughter.
Gill keeps it grave: let Job lay his hand on the beast if he dares, for it is a perilous thing, whale or crocodile.
Clarke gathers Heath and Good — 'strike home, rely not on a second stroke'; 'dare the contest, be firm' — a mortal hazard: kill him at once, or he will kill thee.
Ellicott reads 'remember the battle' as 'bear in mind what thou dost attempt, and thou wilt not do it again.'
Henry turns it to counsel: desist, remember the battle before engaging — and, past the beast, cease the controversy with God and make peace (Isa. 27:4-5).

themes: remember the battle, do no more

schools.summary: Gill reads 'the hope of him' as the hope of mastery — crocodiles and whales have been taken, but the orca never; of such an invincible beast the verse speaks.
Clarke: miss the first advantage and there is no hope, for the sight of the monster dissipates courage; Wesley: 'the hope of taking or conquering him.'
Ellicott reads the vain 'hope' of the rash man who would attack, and the 'sight' of the infuriated crocodile before which the boldest is cast down.
Henry: it is to no purpose to attempt it, for the very sight of the beast will appal and make a stout man faint — the pivot from the creature to the Creator.

themes: the hope of him is in vain
cast down at the sight of him
the hunter overthrown before a blow

schools.summary: Ellicott paraphrases the divine reasoning — 'if the creatures of My hand strike such terror, how far more terrible must I be?' — with an alternative first clause; Keil and Delitzsch render 'none is so foolhardy that he dare excite him,' the very design of the beast-speech.
Clarke presses the use God makes of it: if Job cannot stand against the crocodile, one of the creatures of his hand, how can he resist the Maker?
Gill grounds it in the beast's habit — the crocodile asleep on ground or in water, dangerous to arouse; whales seen asleep like rocks, forty together.
Henry draws the moral: none dares stir up the leviathan, and 'who then is able to stand before God?' — the majesty of the Lord over a rebel man.

themes: who then is able to stand before me

schools.summary: Henry unfolds God's sovereign right — indebted to none, owner of all: 'whatsoever is under the whole heaven is mine,' this leviathan included; 'if I were hungry I would not tell thee' (Ps. 50:12).
Gill: who has first given God anything that was his own? — the very word the apostle presses in Rom. 11:35.
Clarke: 'do I need my creatures? all under the heavens is my property'; Wesley: who can be beforehand with God in kindnesses, since all things are his?
Ellicott judges the appeal fits better at the close of the description than here; Keil and Delitzsch note the Ker that would make the next words a question, 'should I be silent about its members?'

themes: whatsoever is under heaven is mine
God owes nothing and owns everything
the ground of the whole argument

schools.summary: Gill takes 'his parts' as the members, or 'his bars,' the limbs like bars of iron for strength.
Henry reads God's preface to the anatomy and a lesson on beauty — even the leviathan is comely in God's eye; his works appear most excellent when viewed part by part.
Clarke calls the AV 'no just translation'; with Good he reads God's fearlessness of his own handiwork — 'I cannot be confounded at his limbs and violence.'

sides.position: God will not conceal the creature's parts, power, and comely proportion (AV)
'I cannot be confounded at his limbs' — God is nowise daunted by his own work

themes: I will not conceal his parts
the comely proportion of the beast
the Creator undaunted by his work

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'strip off his outer garment,' i.e. his scales, and 'come within his double bridle,' the doubling of the jaw; Keil and Delitzsch take the same view of the doubled jaw.
Gill reads 'discover' as 'uncover,' setting aside Broughton's 'sea as garment'; the garment is the skin or scaly coat none dare flay off.
Wesley: the garment is the skin, the 'double bridle' the fast jaws the Greeks called 'bridles'; Clarke bluntly, 'who can rip up the hide of this terrible monster?'
Henry: who dares come near enough to handle the skin, bridle him like a horse, or reach within jaws like a double bridle?
Gill reads 'the doors of his face' as the folding-door jaws — the crocodile's gape seven feet broad (Peter Martyr), able to hold a whole cow (Leo Africanus); the whale's mouth as vast (Jonah's fish).
Clarke keeps the plain sense: the jaws, 'which are most tremendous.'
Ellicott glosses the phrase as the mouth, and the second clause 'round about his teeth is terror.'
Henry: he who opens the doors of this face sees teeth terrible round about — 'it would make a man tremble to think of having a leg or an arm between them.'
Gill reads the scales as true of the crocodile's impenetrable back, not the smooth whale; and records Aben Ezra, Hasaeus, and Broughton referring 'his pride' to the teeth, strong as a shield.
Wesley: the scales are 'closely compacted, as things fastened by a seal,' true of the crocodile but not the scaleless whale; Clarke, 'impenetrable.'
Henry: the scales are the beast's beauty, strength, and pride, sticking so close that no air pierces (kept warm) and no sword pierces (kept safe).

debates.question: Does 'his pride, the shields,' name the scales or the teeth?

sides.position: the mailed scales of the back and tail
the teeth, strong as a shield

themes: shut up as with a close seal

schools.summary: Gill makes the tightness an argument against the whale (its skin all of a piece); notes the toothed-whale reading (forty or fifty teeth in sockets) but lets the next clause strain it.
Clarke: a musket-ball fired in any direction cannot pass through such scales.
Keil and Delitzsch note the living habit — the crocodile sunning with open jaws, little birds walking in the deadly gape (Herodotus, Dieterici).
Henry: the close scales keep the creature at once warm (no air) and safe (no sword).

themes: no air can come between them
a thing no assault can enter

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the Hebrew 'a man in his brother' — scales fitted as if embracing; 'they cannot be sundered' will not agree with the drawn-apart teeth, only the interlocking plates.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'one upon another they are arranged, they hold fast together, inseparably.'
Henry, reading the three scale-verses as one, presses the security of the knitting — fortified at every point, warmed and warded by Providence.

themes: a wisdom no hand can take to pieces

schools.summary: Gill: those who face the sun are apt to sneeze, and the sunning crocodile's spray shines in the rays; the whale's water-jets glitter like a rainbow.

Clarke reads the spray forming an iris, and the eyes dull under water but sparkling above — whence the Egyptians made the crocodile's eye the emblem of morning (Horapollo, Sophocles, Euripides); Wesley the same, light breaking as after night.
Ellicott reads the eyes as 'fiery red and glowing.'
Henry gathers it under the terror the beast scatters by breath and looks — eyes shining like a flame or the eyelids of morning.

themes: by his neesings a light doth shine
eyes like the eyelids of the morning
the beast rises like the dawn

schools.summary: Gill owns the words hyperbolical but grounds them — the whale's water-jets and the orca's glittering spermaceti; Ovid says as much of the boar.

Clarke leans on Dr. Young — the crocodile's long-pent breath bursts out hot as fire and smoke (Virgil's fiery-nostrilled horse), a caution against thinking Eastern metaphors overdrawn; Wesley: the crocodile breathes a fiery smoke as from a furnace.
Henry lets the hyperbole rise to its aim — to intimate the terror of the wrath of God, whose fiery mouth devours (Ps. 18:8), kindles Tophet (Isa. 30:33), and consumes the wicked one (2 Thess. 2:8).

themes: burning lamps out of his mouth
a figure of the wrath of God

schools.summary: Gill notes the crocodile's likeness to the river-horse in breathing, its large nostrils seeming to fume as out of a furnace.
Ellicott finds the last word uncertain (the 'hook' of v.2), reading 'as of a seething pot and rushes' — a pot driven to the boil by a fire of reeds.
Henry reads the smoke with the flame as one sustained figure of the dreadful heat that shadows the divine wrath.
Gill marks the words plainly hyperbolical, of a piece with the lamps and the smoke.
Wesley: 'kindleth coals' is a hyperbolical expression denoting extraordinary heat.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'his breath kindleth coals, and a flame goeth out of his mouth,' the culmination of the fire-crescendo before the neck.
Henry: the breath that kindles coals is the near likeness of that breath of the Almighty which sets Tophet alight — what the beast does in the flesh the poem means of its Maker.

themes: a flame goeth out of his mouth

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'before him danceth fear' / 'pining sorrow exulteth before him,' a marvellous personification of terror; Keil and Delitzsch 'despair danceth hence before him,' a heart-dissolution that flees at his approach.
Gill takes the neck-strength as a mark against the neckless whale, yet grants Aristotle and Pliny credit the crocodile with a moving neck.

Clarke rejects the AV — the Hebrew is 'destruction exulteth before him,' 'our translation is simply insignificant'; Wesley makes sorrow the beast's companion and harbinger, as fear attends the god of war.
Henry keeps the AV: sorrow rides in triumph before the beast, what is grief to others being dancing to him.

debates.question: How is the second clause to be rendered?

sides.position: 'sorrow is turned into joy before him' — the beast delights in the havoc that grieves all else (AV)
'destruction / despair dances (and flees) before him' — a personification of the terror he spreads

themes: sorrow turned to joy, or terror dancing

schools.summary: Gill: the muscles are neither flaccid nor flabby but solid and firmly compacted, a body without a soft place.
Ellicott: the parts that hang loose in other beasts (dewlaps) are here drawn tight; Keil and Delitzsch: even the fleshy flanks cling close and cannot be moved.
Clarke: the flesh is 'strongly and firmly compacted.'
Henry: 'he is as if he were all bone' — a flesh of very brass, set against Job's own complaint that his flesh was not brass (ch. 6:12).

themes: the flakes of his flesh joined
the frail man against the unyielding beast

schools.summary: Gill: the hardness is of the heart's qualities, not its substance — bold, undaunted, unmerciful, true of the crocodile especially (Aelianus).
Ellicott reads 'heart' as the beast's nature or disposition, a courage nothing appals, not the physical organ.
Clarke and Wesley on the nether millstone — made harder and stronger than the upper because it bears the weight and the grinding.
Henry: the beast has spirit equal to his strength, bulky yet sprightly; as the skin cannot be pierced, so the courage cannot be daunted.

themes: his heart firm as a stone
the picture of the fearless sinner

schools.summary: Gill keeps the clear half: the beast rears above the surface, its bulk and jaws seen, and the sight dismays the boldest.
Wesley reads 'breakings' as distress (Ps. 60:2; Jonah 2:4) and 'purify themselves' of men driven by terror to cry to God and purge their consciences.
Henry the same devout way: the mighty betake themselves to prayers, confess their sins, and get ready for death, as the seafarers of ch. 3:8.
Ellicott turns it the other way: 'they purify themselves' means the terror-struck take themselves off, withdrawing as men unclean — a flight, not a repentance.

debates.question: What is meant by 'they purify themselves' at the rising of the beast?

sides.position: the terrified turn to God, cry to him, and purge their consciences
they are beside themselves and withdraw as men set apart for uncleanness — a flight, not repentance

outliers.note: Confesses that no version, ancient or modern, has understood the verse, and its true sense is not known — setting the LXX, Good, Heath, and Coverdale side by side in honest doubt.

themes: by reason of breakings they purify themselves

schools.summary: Gill: the sword breaks or cannot lodge; the harpoon cannot enter the scaled crocodile though it wounds the whale, so this verse and the rest suit the crocodile.
Ellicott renders 'as to one approaching him to slay him, his sword cannot stand; it will snap in his hand.'
Wesley: the sword 'cannot endure the stroke'; Clarke glosses the 'habergeon' as the Norman hauberk of linked rings (Neh. 4:16).
Henry reads the verse with the three following as one catalogue of futile arms, the beast an image of the hard-hearted sinner who scorns the threatenings of God.

themes: lay down the sword of controversy

schools.summary: Gill: a straw may as well be cast as an iron bar, for nothing marks the steeled back; Eustathius says the sharpest iron is turned and blunted upon him.
Keil and Delitzsch carry the invincibility toward the under-parts, the belly set with the sharpest shards spreading a threshing-sledge upon the mire.
Henry: iron and brass are to him as straw and rotten wood, and he laughs at them — the hard heart that makes light of every threatening.

themes: cease from striving before such a power

schools.summary: Gill: the crocodile's skin cannot be pierced with arrows (Peter Martyr), so it neither fears them nor flees.
Henry: the darts, arrows, and sling-stones that wound from afar do the beast no damage, nature having armed him at all points.

themes: the arrow cannot make him flee
no complaint drives the Maker from his purpose

schools.summary: Gill suspects a wall-battering engine here (Ben Gersom), of no avail against the beast.
Ellicott would render the word 'clubs,' adding the bludgeon to the useless arms.

Clarke tells of a twelve-foot crocodile, starved thirty-five days with its mouth tied, that overturned a bale of coffee and six men with one blow of its tail — 'what power, then, must lodge in one twenty feet long!'
Henry: all the offensive weapons of men are no terror to him; he laughs at the shaking of the spear.

themes: he laugheth at the shaking of a spear

schools.summary: Gill: sharp stones under him give no pain, so hard is the hide that meets them.
Clarke: splinters of flint are to him as the softest reeds; Wesley: the sharpest stones and shells are as easy to him as the mire.
Ellicott: 'he spreadeth, as it were, a threshing-wain upon the mire' — his under parts a pointed surface printing the ground; Keil and Delitzsch, the belly furnished with the sharpest shards.

themes: proof against hurt, and edged like a harrow
no point of vantage against the beast

schools.summary: Gill reads the boiling of the deep as the beast's violent agitation, and thinks it suits the whale better than the less vehement crocodile.

Clarke: the froth rises like the scum of ointment, though the crocodile's musk-scent may make the comparison literal; Wesley: the Nile is called a sea (Isa. 11:15), as Euphrates the sea of Babylon (Isa. 21:1), the crocodile at home in such waters.
Ellicott: 'the sea' need not mean salt water, the Nile being still called the sea by the Arabs, like the 'sea-wall' of the Thames.
Henry keeps the plain image: the beast's motion puts the water into a ferment, a froth as on a pot of boiling ointment.

themes: he maketh the deep to boil like a pot
the sea like a pot of ointment
a power that troubles the deep

schools.summary: Gill reads the shining path as the white froth or oily matter of the beast's passage, whales ploughing a glittering furrow a German mile long.
Wesley: the path shines with froth and foam, as in a ship's wake by night; Clarke tells of watching a phosphoric wake become a stream of fire, millions of particles struck from the water.
Henry: it makes a shining path such as even a ship does not, so that one may trace the beast by its bubbles (cf. Prov. 30:19), yet dare not come near.

themes: he maketh a path to shine after him

schools.summary: Gill: most sea-creatures have a counterpart on land (the crocodile a likeness in the lizard), but for bulk and terror the leviathan stands alone, as the Targum confesses.
Clarke: no beast so dangerous, strong, and hard to slay; 'made without fear' — no creature acquainted with man so wholly destitute of fear as the crocodile.
Henry: a non-such, his dominion in the waters not the land — a mercy he is so confined and watched (ch. 7:12) — with courage bred in his very frame.

themes: upon earth there is not his like
an image of the Maker's power

schools.summary: Henry reads the beast beholding all high things with contempt, 'a king over all the children of pride' (so Mr. Caryl), but grants the alternative that God is the King over the proud, taming behemoth (ch. 40:19) and leviathan (ch. 40:11-13; Isa. 2:11).
Gill reads the clause of God, who beholds all high things and abases every proud one — doing what Job could not — so that Job must own his sovereignty.

Wesley: God tames both beasts and is King over all the children of pride, brutal or rational; Clarke lays out Calmet's Egypt-and-Pharaoh, Houbigant's Satan, and the reading of 'men,' ending in doubt what leviathan is.

debates.question: Who is the subject of 'he beholdeth all high things, a king over all the children of pride'?

sides.position: the leviathan itself, the proudest of proud beasts
God, who beholds every proud one and abases him
the literal crocodile of the Nile
an emblem of Egypt, the crocodile-king Pharaoh
a figure of Satan, king over the sons of pride
a creature now unknown, perhaps an extinct monster of the waters

outliers.note: Doubts whether whale or crocodile is meant at all, half-inclines to some extinct monster of the waters, and confesses plainly, 'we have yet to learn what leviathan is.'

themes: king over all the children of pride
the beast or God as subject
